title.rendered: EV Thermal Management Control Strategy: How Compressor, Expansion Valve and Fan Work Together

content.rendered:
Thermal Management Control Strategies for Electric Vehicles: How Compressors, Expansion Valves and Fans Work Together

The success or failure of a thermal management system hinges on its control strategy, rather than solely on the components themselves. Even with the world’s most advanced electric compressor, poor control logic can still lead to energy wastage, accelerated wear and tear on equipment, and even cause the battery to fall outside its ideal operating temperature range. However, current explanations of thermal management in electric vehicles often fall into two extremes: either academic papers brimming with mathematical formulas from control theory, or simple hobbyist projects involving nothing more than an Arduino connected to a relay.

This article aims to provide a middle ground that better meets the practical needs of frontline engineers. There are three core actuators in an electric vehicle’s thermal management system—the compressor, the electronic expansion valve and the fan—each of which responds to different control signals. We will analyse these three control loops in plain, accessible language: what parameters each loop monitors, which components it drives, and why they need to work in concert.

The Three Key Actuators and Their Core Control Objectives

Before exploring the control loops, let us first clarify the role of each actuator. Each actuator in the refrigeration circuit is responsible for controlling just one key parameter:

  • Compressor: Responsible for controlling the cooling capacity. Its rotational speed determines the mass flow rate of the refrigerant within the circuit. The higher the speed, the more heat is transferred per unit of time; conversely, the lower the speed, the less heat is transferred. The operation of all other components in the system depends on the compressor’s action.
  • Electronic Expansion Valve (EXV): Responsible for controlling the distribution of the refrigerant. Its opening determines the flow of refrigerant entering the evaporator, which in turn determines the ‘superheat’ at the evaporator outlet—that is, the difference between the actual temperature of the refrigerant and the temperature at which it begins to condense back into a liquid.
  • Fan: Responsible for controlling heat dissipation capacity. Its speed determines the efficiency with which the condenser dissipates heat into the ambient air. Without airflow, condensation cannot occur, and the entire refrigeration cycle will consequently come to a standstill.

This ‘three-way division of labour’ architecture is not our own invention. In peer-reviewed research on ‘demand-based heat pump control’ (published by MDPI), the benchmark control algorithm employs the same logic: one PI loop is used to regulate the compressor speed, one PI loop maintains the superheat at the evaporator outlet via the expansion valve, and another PI loop controls the fan airflow. We mention this to validate the soundness of this analytical framework—this article will not delve into complex transfer function derivations.

For system designers, the core logic is actually quite simple: three actuators, three signals, three control loops.

Loop 1 – Compressor speed regulated by water temperature

Logic: The compressor speed is adjusted based on the difference between the system water temperature and the target temperature. When the water temperature is higher than the target temperature, the speed increases; when the water temperature drops, the speed decreases.

Why use water temperature as the reference? Because water temperature is the most direct indicator of the system’s cooling demand. The water (or water-ethylene glycol mixture) circuit is responsible for dissipating heat from the battery and power electronics; its temperature reflects the system’s current cooling demand in real time. Regulating via water temperature ensures that cooling output remains in sync with actual demand: the compressor will only run at full speed when the system genuinely requires maximum cooling capacity.

Another scenario—and one that this circuit is designed to avoid—is ‘stop-start’ operation: allowing the compressor to run at full speed until a certain threshold is reached, then switching it off, only to restart it later. Each start-up generates an inrush current, causing bearing wear and injecting an unregulated surge of refrigerant into the circuit. Continuous speed regulation, however, avoids all these issues. Whilst this approach does indeed save energy, this is merely a secondary benefit; from the perspective of improving reliability alone, the installation of this circuit is already essential.

Engineering insight: When selecting a compressor, its capacity should be determined based on the most extreme operating conditions (worst-case scenario); however, during actual operation, the ‘water temperature control circuit’ should determine the specific capacity required at any given moment. In other words, the aim is to achieve ‘capacity on demand’ rather than ‘default full output’.

Circuit 2 — Expansion Valve Control Based on Superheat

Logic: The opening of the expansion valve is adjusted according to the superheat. A higher superheat results in a greater opening; a lower superheat results in a smaller opening.

What is ‘superheat’? It is the difference between the temperature of the refrigerant at the evaporator outlet and the saturation temperature at which that refrigerant begins to condense. In other words, it represents the safety margin ensuring the refrigerant remains in a ‘completely gaseous’ state before any undesirable liquid component appears.

Importance: Superheat is the most critical safety variable in a refrigeration circuit; improper control can lead to serious consequences:

  • Too low: Liquid refrigerant enters the compressor inlet. Compressors are designed to compress gaseous refrigerant, whereas liquids are incompressible; if ‘liquid slugging’ occurs, the compressor may be destroyed within seconds. The primary purpose of this control circuit is precisely to prevent such catastrophic failure.
  • Too high: Insufficient liquid supply to the evaporator—the majority of its heat exchange area is then utilised solely for superheating the vapour, rather than for the heat absorption associated with the boiling of liquid refrigerant (which is key to the actual refrigeration process). In this scenario, although the system is operating and consuming power, the cooling performance is poor.

Industry practice: In relevant control research literature, the target superheat value at the evaporator outlet is often set at around 5 K (a design scheme based on demand control published by MDPI adopts this value). This should be regarded merely as a reference point rather than a fixed specification; the actual target value must be calibrated according to the specific project, the type of refrigerant used, and the range of operating conditions.

Advanced techniques worth understanding: An excellent control scheme does not rely solely on superheat feedback. A common approach (as described in the control scheme for automotive electronic expansion valves in patent CN103245154B) is to introduce compressor speed as a ‘feedforward’ signal to pre-adjust the expansion valve opening, and then superimpose superheat feedback for fine-tuning. When the compressor speed increases, the system can anticipate an increase in refrigerant flow and thus increase the valve opening in advance, without having to wait for a deviation in superheat to occur before making a correction. In this scenario, the feedback loop need only handle minor deviations—which means smaller correction amplitudes, reduced system oscillations and more precise control.

This also provides the strongest technical justification for integrating the compressor control loop and the electronic expansion valve (EXV) control loop within a single controller: feedforward control requires real-time access to the compressor’s speed signal. When this signal is transmitted between two separate controllers, it is exchanged via the CAN bus—which involves communication delays and message scheduling, and where calibration work is often divided between two different teams. If the signals are housed within a single controller, they interact via shared memory. This mechanism for coordinating loops, which is necessary for implementing feedforward control, is a characteristic at the system architecture level, rather than merely a software function.

Loop 3 — Fan speed regulation based on condenser pressure

Logical explanation: The control of the condenser fan is based on the pressure on the high-pressure side of the condenser. For example, when the high-pressure side pressure reaches approximately 13 bar, the fan starts; the specific start/stop pressure thresholds and fan speed curves must be calibrated according to the specific vehicle project.

Why choose pressure rather than temperature? The pressure on the high-pressure side directly reflects the condensing load, i.e. the amount of heat the condenser currently needs to dissipate. The response speed of the pressure signal is far faster than that of a temperature sensor—which is subject to the thermal inertia of the heat exchanger and therefore exhibits lag. Pressure is a leading indicator, whilst temperature is a lagging indicator. Controlling the fan based on pressure means that the fan can respond instantly to changes in load, rather than waiting until heat has already accumulated before acting.

Regarding calibration: the aforementioned value of 13 bar is merely an example. In actual projects, the setting of start-stop pressure thresholds and fan speed curves must take into account the specifications and dimensions of the vehicle’s condenser, environmental conditions and noise requirements. For example, the pressure control strategy (mapping table) for a coach operating in a 45°C environment will inevitably differ from that of similar hardware operating in a milder climate. This constitutes standard calibration work during project development, and any professional controller supplier should provide the necessary support.

Please note the common pattern across these three loops: the control variable on which each actuator is based is the parameter most directly related to its own function—the compressor is modulated according to refrigeration demand (coolant temperature), the valves are modulated according to the state of the refrigerant (superheat), and the fan is modulated according to the heat rejection load (condensing pressure). None of the loops relies solely on ‘proxy indicators’ that are far removed from the target variable to implement inferential control.

Why the three control loops should be integrated into a single controller

There is a coupling between these three control loops, and it is precisely this coupling that provides the fundamental rationale for integration:

  • Changes in compressor speed → Changes in refrigerant mass flow rate → Shift in superheat → The electronic expansion valve (EXV) loop must respond.
  • Changes in the electronic expansion valve opening → fluctuations in evaporator pressure → consequent changes in condenser pressure → the fan circuit must respond.
  • Changes in fan speed → fluctuations in condenser pressure → changes in compressor discharge conditions → a shift in the operating point of the compressor circuit.

The output of each circuit acts as a disturbance for the other circuits. If these circuits are managed separately by different controllers, they must be coordinated via the vehicle’s CAN bus: this involves message queuing, delays of tens of milliseconds, and independent commissioning of each circuit by different suppliers. Although this approach is certainly feasible—and has been the industry standard for many years—this coordination mechanism is inherently at odds with the system architecture itself.

With a single integrated controller, the circuits can share sensor data directly and operate under a unified timing reference; feedforward paths (such as feeding the compressor speed signal into the electronic expansion valve circuit) incur virtually no delay. Control strategies and hardware architecture can complement rather than hinder one another. Furthermore, this integration reduces system costs by minimising the number of housings, wiring harnesses and validation efforts. We have analysed this in detail in another article discussing ‘How an integrated thermal management controller reduces system costs’.

As for concerns regarding ‘flexibility’, the answer remains the same as ever: the CAN protocol, CAN IDs, baud rates and the control logic itself can still be customised for specific projects; the controller can also be adapted to the technical specifications of the compressor and motor selected by the customer. Integration achieves standardisation of the infrastructure, not the standardisation of project-specific decisions.

Three Control Errors Leading to Energy Waste

Based on our experience in supporting vehicle integration projects, the majority of energy waste in poorly commissioned thermal management systems stems from the following three control errors. It is worth noting that each error corresponds directly to a missing or improperly commissioned control loop:

  1. ‘Hunting’ of the electronic expansion valve. The valve opening fluctuates constantly—opening, overshooting, closing, undershooting—and is never able to stabilise at the target position. A typical cause is an improperly tuned superheat control loop: if the response is too aggressive, the system will exhibit hunting; if the response is too sluggish, the superheat may deviate from the normal range and enter the dangerous zone mentioned earlier. ‘Hunting’ leads to a twofold waste of energy: the compressor is constantly responding to ever-changing target operating conditions, whilst the evaporator is unable to operate at its point of highest efficiency.
  2. Frequent compressor start-stop cycles (short-cycling). The compressor repeatedly switches between full-speed operation and a stopped state, sometimes occurring several times per minute. The root cause lies in the lack of a continuous speed regulation mechanism—or, to put it another way, the water temperature control loop that should have been installed has not actually been implemented, resulting in the system having to rely solely on crude ‘on/off’ thresholds for control. Each start-up generates an inrush current and causes mechanical wear; the solution is to introduce the proportional speed control described in ‘Loop 1’.
  3. The fan always runs at full speed. Regardless of the load—even in winter, under low-load conditions or at night—the condenser fan always operates at full speed. The reason for this is the lack of a pressure-based control mechanism: due to the absence of ‘Loop 3’, the fan cannot receive load signals and is therefore forced to default to the ‘full-speed operation’ mode, which, whilst safe, is extremely wasteful. In coach applications, the condenser fan running at full speed means a continuous power consumption in the kilowatt range, which in most cases yields no practical benefit.

If you have identified the above issues in your existing system, simply replacing components with larger ones is not usually the solution. The crux of the problem often lies in the fact that certain control loops have not been properly established (i.e. the control loops are not closed).

Please provide the technical specifications of your compressor, motor parameters and system objectives (including cooling capacity, operating ambient temperature range and type of refrigerant used). We will recommend a control logic configuration and provide an objective analysis of the associated trade-offs; at the same time, we will identify which standard control loops require targeted calibration to meet your specific project requirements.
